functions.name: sns.kdeplot()
functions.explanation: A KDE (Kernel Density Estimate) plot is a data visualization that shows the probability distribution of a continuous variable. It works like a smoothed, continuous version of a histogram, where every individual data point contributes a small, rounded "bump" (a kernel). Adding these bumps together creates a single, smooth curve.

functions.name: df.select_dtypes(include="object/number")
functions.explanation: Selected columns of a certain datatype. Usually assigned to a variable to store it for analysis by datatype.

functions.name: df.dtypes
functions.explanation: Shows data type for each column of a dataframe
functions.example:
Example Output:

functions.name: .round()
functions.explanation: Round to a number of decimals

functions.name: df.head()
functions.explanation: Returns the first 5 rows (or n rows) of a DataFrame. First thing you run on any new dataset.

functions.name: df.info()
functions.explanation: Prints column dtypes, non-null counts, and memory usage. Use to spot missing data or wrong types fast.

functions.name: df.describe()
functions.explanation: Summary stats (count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max) for numeric columns.
functions.example:
df.describe()
df.describe(include='all')  # include categorical too

df['COLUMN'].describe() # select a column

functions.name: df.shape
functions.explanation: Returns (rows, columns) as a tuple. No parentheses — it's an attribute, not a method.

functions.name: df.columns
functions.explanation: Returns the column labels as an Index object. Useful for checking names or looping over columns.

functions.name: df.isnull()
functions.explanation: Returns a same-shaped DataFrame of booleans marking where values are NaN/None.

functions.name: df.isnull().sum()
functions.explanation: Counts missing values per column — the standard first check for data quality.

functions.name: df.fillna()
functions.explanation: Replaces NaN values with a specified value, method, or per-column mapping.

functions.name: df.dropna()
functions.explanation: Removes rows (or columns) containing NaN values. Use subset= to target specific columns.

functions.name: df['new'] = ...
functions.explanation: Creates or overwrites a column by assigning a Series, scalar, or computed expression.

functions.name: df.apply()
functions.explanation: Applies a function along an axis (rows or columns). Slower than vectorised ops but flexible for custom logic.
functions.example: df['risk_band'] = df['score'].apply(lambda s: 'high' if s < 600 else 'low')

functions.name: df.applymap()
functions.explanation: Applies a function element-wise to every cell of a DataFrame (not Series-aware). Deprecated in newer pandas in favour of df.map().
functions.example: df.applymap(lambda x: round(x, 2) if isinstance(x, float) else x)

functions.name: pd.cut()
functions.explanation: Bins continuous values into discrete intervals you define — classic for credit score bands.

functions.name: pd.qcut()
functions.explanation: Bins values into quantile-based buckets (equal-sized groups) rather than fixed-width ranges.

functions.name: pd.to_datetime()
functions.explanation: Converts a column of strings/numbers into proper datetime objects so you can use .dt accessors.

functions.name: df['col'].dt.year
functions.explanation: Extracts the year (or .month, .day, .dayofweek etc.) from a datetime column.

functions.name: df['a'] + df['b']
functions.explanation: Vectorised element-wise addition between two columns — fast, no loop needed.

functions.name: df['a'] - df['b']
functions.explanation: Vectorised element-wise subtraction between two columns.

functions.name: df['a'] * df['b']
functions.explanation: Vectorised element-wise multiplication between two columns.

functions.name: df['a'] / df['b']
functions.explanation: Vectorised element-wise division. Watch for divide-by-zero producing inf/NaN.

functions.name: df.add()
functions.explanation: Method form of addition, useful because it supports a fill_value for missing data instead of producing NaN.

functions.name: df['col']
functions.explanation: Selects a single column as a Series.

functions.name: df.loc[]
functions.explanation: Label-based indexing — select rows/columns by index label or boolean mask.

functions.name: df.iloc[]
functions.explanation: Position-based indexing — select rows/columns by integer position, like numpy slicing.

functions.name: df.query()
functions.explanation: Filters rows using a string expression — often more readable than chained boolean masks.

functions.name: df.filter()
functions.explanation: Selects columns or rows by label pattern (e.g. regex or substring), not by value.

functions.name: df.groupby()
functions.explanation: Splits the DataFrame into groups by key(s) so you can aggregate/transform within each group.

functions.name: df.agg()
functions.explanation: Applies one or more aggregation functions, often after groupby, including different functions per column.

functions.name: df.transform()
functions.explanation: Like agg, but returns a result the same shape as the input — great for group-relative features.

functions.name: pd.merge()
functions.explanation: SQL-style join between two DataFrames on key column(s).

functions.name: df.join()
functions.explanation: Joins DataFrames primarily on their index rather than a column key.

functions.name: pd.concat()
functions.explanation: Stacks DataFrames together along an axis (rows by default), e.g. combining batches of data.

functions.name: df.pivot_table()
functions.explanation: Reshapes data into a spreadsheet-style pivot with aggregation built in.

functions.name: df.sort_values()
functions.explanation: Sorts rows by one or more column values.

functions.name: df.sort_index()
functions.explanation: Sorts rows (or columns) by their index labels rather than values.

functions.name: df.corr()
functions.explanation: Computes pairwise correlation between numeric columns — useful for spotting multicollinearity before modelling.

functions.name: df.mean()
functions.explanation: Computes the mean of numeric columns (or a Series).

functions.name: df.std()
functions.explanation: Computes the standard deviation of numeric columns (or a Series).

snippets.title: Histogram with labelled, dollar-formatted axes
snippets.description: Base histogram, but with axis labels and $-formatted ticks instead of matplotlib's default 1e6 scientific notation — useful any time you're plotting a currency column.
snippets.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker

ax = df['AMT_CREDIT'].hist(bins=50)  # plot histogram, capture the Axes object
ax.set_xlabel("Credit Amount ($)")   # label x-axis
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")           # label y-axis (histograms show counts, not density)

# Reformat x-axis ticks: 1000000 -> "$1,000,000" instead of "1e6"
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f'${x:,.0f}'))
plt.show()

snippets.title: Axis tick formatting — readable numbers on any plot
snippets.description: Overrides matplotlib's default tick labels (which switch to 1e6-style scientific notation for large numbers) with custom formatted text. Works on any matplotlib/seaborn axis — bar charts, scatter plots, histograms, not just KDE.
snippets.code:
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker  # gives us FuncFormatter, for custom tick labels

ax.set_xlabel("Credit Amount ($)")  # override default x-axis label
ax.set_ylabel("Density")            # override default y-axis label

# Reformat every x-axis tick: raw number -> "$" + comma-separated + no decimals
# e.g. 1000000 -> "$1,000,000" instead of matplotlib's default "1e6"
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f'${x:,.0f}'))

plt.show()  # render the plot

snippets.title: KDE Plot — comparing distributions between groups
snippets.description: Shows the shape of a numeric variable's distribution, split into separate curves per category. Each curve is normalised independently (common_norm=False), so you're comparing shape, not raw counts — useful for spotting whether two groups (e.g. defaulters vs non-defaulters) differ in distribution, but doesn't tell you rate/probability by itself.
snippets.code:
import seaborn as sns

# KDE plot of AMT_CREDIT, split into separate curves by TARGET (0=repaid, 1=defaulted)
# common_norm=False -> each curve normalised independently, so shapes are comparable
# regardless of how imbalanced the two groups are
ax = sns.kdeplot(data=df, x="AMT_CREDIT", hue="TARGET", common_norm=False)

snippets.title: Correlation Heatmap
snippets.description: Correlation heatmap for columns in a data frame. Create a subset for large dataframes for readability.
snippets.code:
# import seaborn as sns
# import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
# import numpy as np

corr = df.corr(numeric_only=True)
mask = np.eye(len(corr), dtype=bool)

n = len(corr)
plt.figure(figsize=(n * 0.5, n * 0.5))  # scale figure size to number of columns
sns.heatmap(
    corr, mask=mask, cmap='RdYlGn', vmin=-1, vmax=1,
    annot=True, fmt='.2f', annot_kws={'size': 7}, linewidths=0.5,
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

snippets.title: Missing value audit
snippets.description: Quick audit of null counts and percentages across all columns, sorted worst first.
snippets.code:
null_counts = df.isnull().sum()
null_pct = (null_counts / len(df) * 100).round(2)
audit = pd.DataFrame({'nulls': null_counts, 'pct': null_pct})
audit = audit[audit['nulls'] > 0].sort_values('pct', ascending=False)
print(audit)
